title: The conquest of Mecca
hook: the Prophet ﷺ enters Mecca with ten thousand, almost without fighting, head bowed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khaybar and Safiyyah, a chief's daughter honored for her family. Your line was a mother of believers. Did you honor someone's background today? Day two hundred seventy-seven.

Eight years ago, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ slipped out of Mecca by night, hunted, with a price on his head. He looked back at the city and said he loved it, and would never have left if its people hadn't driven him out. Now it's Ramadan again. Mecca's allies have broken the peace of Hudaybiyyah, attacking a tribe allied to the Muslims. And one night the people of Mecca look out from the hills and see the valley below covered in campfires. Ten thousand of them, maybe more. The man they drove out has come back. Everyone in the city knows what conquerors do. Today: the conquest of Mecca.
screen: `EIGHT YEARS AGO, BY NIGHT.` → `THE PEACE IS BROKEN.` → `TEN THOUSAND CAMPFIRES.`

segments.voice: That night, Abu Sufyan, Mecca's leader, the enemy of twenty years, came out to see the camp, and before morning he had become Muslim. And the Prophet made him an offer to carry back to the city, recorded in Sahih Muslim: whoever enters Abu Sufyan's house is safe. Whoever shuts his own door is safe. Whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe. In other words: stay home, and nothing will happen to you. Then the army entered from several sides. One commander called out, today is the day of slaughter, and the Prophet took the banner from him and said, the early biographers report: today is the day of mercy. There was a brief clash on one side of the city. Otherwise, Mecca was entered almost without a fight. And the Prophet himself? The biographers describe him riding in on his camel with his head bowed so low, in humility before God, that his beard nearly touched the saddle. A companion in Sahih al-Bukhari remembered him reciting Surah al-Fath, the Victory, softly, as he rode. The surah that came after Hudaybiyyah, when it all looked like losing. He went to the Kaaba. Around it stood some three hundred and sixty idols, and he pushed them over with a stick, one by one, reciting: truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Then Bilal, the formerly enslaved man once tortured in this very city, climbed onto the roof of the Kaaba and called the adhan. He had come home as a conqueror, and he came home bowing.
screen: `WHOEVER SHUTS HIS DOOR IS SAFE.` · `TODAY IS THE DAY OF MERCY.` · `HEAD BOWED, RECITING AL-FATH.` · `BILAL ON THE ROOF OF THE KAABA.` · then, large: `HEAD BOWED ON THE CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enter a room humbly. Sit, and picture the next room you'll walk into where you have some standing: your team, your family, a class you teach, a place where people wait on your word. Picture yourself walking in the way the Prophet rode into Mecca: head a little lowered, voice soft, not taking up more space than you need. If you pray, you can remember that every win is God's. The bell holds the time.
The conquest of Mecca. The Prophet's return to the city that drove him out, with ten thousand, almost without fighting, and his head bowed. Today's word.
Your line: head bowed on the camel. Today, when you get something you wanted, receive it quietly, with your head a little lower. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the conquest of Mecca, in Ramadan of the eighth year, as the moment the Kaaba was cleared of idols and returned to the worship of one God, and it's often told as a lesson in humility and mercy in victory.

fork.setup: you've come back with ten thousand to the city that drove you out. one of your commanders shouts: today is the day of slaughter. what do you do?
options: take the banner and say: today is the day of mercy.
fork.reveal: the Prophet took the banner from him: today is the day of mercy. whoever shut his door was safe.

original.note: Arabic: the opening of Mecca. fath, the same word as al-Fath, the Victory.

trapdoor: what you thought: an army takes a city.
what it means: a return almost without fighting, safety for anyone who stayed home, and a leader riding in with his head bowed.
what a scholar hears: in Arabic it's the fath of Mecca, an opening; Muslim 1780 gives the safe-conduct, Bukhari 4281 the recitation of al-Fath, 4287 the idols.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1780 (whoever enters Abu Sufyan's house, shuts his door, or enters the mosque is safe)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4281 (reciting Surah al-Fath on his camel)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4287 (the idols around the Kaaba; truth has come)
Qur'an 17:81 (truth has come and falsehood has vanished)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): head bowed; the day of mercy; Bilal's adhan on the Kaaba
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3925 (the Prophet's words of love for Mecca on leaving)

notes: The commander who said 'the day of slaughter' was Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah; unnamed in the script. The 'day of mercy' reply is in the sirah (and partly in Bukhari 4280); confirm.
The brief clash (Khalid ibn al-Walid's column) is mentioned without detail; a few people were excluded from the amnesty, which the script doesn't mention. Keeper to decide whether to add.
'Eight years ago' counts from the Hijrah (1 AH to 8 AH); confirm.
Tomorrow's forgiveness speech ('go, you are free') is deliberately not told today.
